Week 10 — Clustering, Segmentation, and Unsupervised Learning for Economics

Week 10 — Unsupervised Learning: Discovering Hidden Patterns in Economic Data

Weeks 8 and 9 focused on:

  • supervised learning
  • prediction
  • classification
  • labeled outcomes

This week introduces:

unsupervised learning

This is a major conceptual shift.

In supervised learning:

  • we know the correct answers
  • models learn from labeled outcomes

In unsupervised learning:

  • there are no predefined labels
  • models attempt to identify hidden structure in data

This week introduces:

  • clustering
  • segmentation
  • similarity
  • dimensionality reduction
  • exploratory pattern discovery

Students will learn:

  • how algorithms group observations
  • how clusters emerge
  • why segmentation matters
  • why unsupervised learning can both reveal and distort patterns

Critical Conceptual Goal

Students must understand:

Clustering does not “discover truth.”

Clusters are:

  • statistical groupings
  • shaped by variables
  • sensitive to assumptions
  • dependent on scale and preprocessing

This week is about:

analytical exploration, not certainty

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this week, students should be able to:

  • explain unsupervised learning
  • distinguish supervised vs unsupervised learning
  • explain clustering intuition
  • understand similarity and distance
  • perform K-Means clustering
  • visualize clusters
  • interpret cluster structure
  • explain dimensionality reduction
  • apply PCA
  • critically evaluate clustering limitations

2. What Is Unsupervised Learning?

Unsupervised learning attempts to identify structure in unlabeled data.

Important Distinction

Supervised Learning

Data + Correct Answers → Learn Relationship

Unsupervised Learning

Data Only → Discover Structure

Example

Suppose we have data on countries:

  • inflation
  • GDP growth
  • debt
  • unemployment
  • reserves

Unsupervised learning may group countries into:

  • stable economies
  • crisis economies
  • high-growth economies

without predefined labels.

Important Lesson

The algorithm is NOT discovering:

natural truth

It is organizing observations based on:

statistical similarity

3. Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning

This distinction is fundamental.

Important Comparison

Supervised Unsupervised
Prediction Exploration
Known labels No labels
Target variable No target
Accuracy evaluation Structural interpretation

Example

Supervised Learning

Predict poverty status

Unsupervised Learning

Identify household groups automatically

Important Lesson

Unsupervised learning is often:

  • exploratory
  • interpretive
  • assumption-sensitive

4. What Is Clustering?

Clustering groups similar observations together.

Example

Suppose firms have:

  • sales
  • profits
  • debt
  • productivity

Clustering may identify:

  • high-performing firms
  • struggling firms
  • medium-risk firms

Important Intuition

Observations within clusters should be:

more similar to each other

than observations in other clusters.

Critical Lesson

Clustering is:

  • exploratory
  • probabilistic
  • sensitive to assumptions

5. Why Clustering Matters in Economics

Economists frequently classify observations into groups.

Applications

Clustering is used for:

  • market segmentation
  • household typologies
  • country classification
  • poverty mapping
  • labor market segmentation
  • consumer analytics
  • policy targeting

Example

A development agency may identify:

  • highly vulnerable districts
  • moderately vulnerable districts
  • resilient districts

using clustering techniques.

Important Warning

Cluster labels are created by analysts.

They are NOT objective truths.

6. Similarity and Distance

Clustering depends on similarity.

Algorithms measure:

how “close” observations are

Example Intuition

Two households may be similar if:

  • income is similar
  • education is similar
  • household size is similar

Distance Concept

Clustering algorithms often use:

Euclidean distance

Simple Intuition

Distance Meaning
Short distance Greater similarity
Large distance Less similarity

Important Lesson

Variable scaling matters enormously.

A variable with large values may dominate clustering.

Example Problem

Suppose:

Variable Scale
Inflation 5–50
GDP 1000–500000

GDP may dominate clustering unfairly.

Important Lesson

Preprocessing matters greatly.

7. Introduction to K-Means Clustering

K-Means is one of the most widely used clustering algorithms.

Basic Idea

The algorithm:

  1. chooses cluster centers
  2. assigns observations
  3. updates centers
  4. repeats until stable

Important Intuition

K-Means attempts to minimize:

within-cluster variation

Example

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

Train Model

kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3)

kmeans.fit(X)

Extract Cluster Labels

clusters = kmeans.labels_

Important Lesson

The analyst chooses:

number of clusters

That choice matters enormously.

8. Choosing Number of Clusters

One of the hardest questions:

How many clusters should exist?

There is NO universally correct answer.

Example

Should countries be grouped into:

  • 2 clusters?
  • 3 clusters?
  • 5 clusters?

Different choices create different narratives.

Elbow Method Intuition

We examine:

how clustering quality changes as cluster number increases

Example

inertia = []

Important Lesson

Cluster selection is partly:

  • statistical
  • analytical
  • interpretive

Critical Warning

Students should avoid:

blindly searching for “the correct” number of clusters

9. Visualizing Clusters

Visualization helps interpret clusters.

Example Scatter Plot

plt.scatter(data["Inflation"],
            data["GDP_Growth"],
            c=clusters)

plt.show()

Interpretation Questions

Ask:

  • Which groups emerge?
  • Are clusters clearly separated?
  • Are observations overlapping?
  • Which observations appear unusual?

Important Warning

Visual separation may appear stronger than reality.

10. Cluster Interpretation

Clusters are useful only if interpreted meaningfully.

Example

Cluster Characteristics
Cluster 1 Low inflation, stable growth
Cluster 2 High inflation, recession
Cluster 3 Moderate growth, moderate inflation

Important Lesson

Interpretation requires:

  • economics
  • context
  • judgment

Algorithms alone do NOT provide meaning.

11. Introduction to Dimensionality Reduction

Many datasets contain:

  • many variables
  • high-dimensional structure

Dimensionality reduction simplifies complexity.

Important Idea

We attempt to:

  • preserve information
  • reduce dimensions

Example

Instead of:

20 variables

we summarize patterns using:

2 or 3 dimensions

Why Useful?

Dimensionality reduction helps:

  • visualization
  • interpretation
  • compression
  • noise reduction

12. PCA Intuition

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is one of the most important dimensionality reduction methods.

Intuition

PCA identifies:

major directions of variation

Example

Suppose:

  • inflation
  • depreciation
  • debt
  • reserves

all move together during crises.

PCA may summarize this as:

one crisis dimension

Important Warning

PCA components are:

mathematical constructs

Interpretation requires caution.

PCA Example

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

Fit PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=2)

principal_components = pca.fit_transform(X)

13. Visualizing High-Dimensional Data

PCA allows visualization of high-dimensional data in two dimensions.

Example

plt.scatter(principal_components[:,0],
            principal_components[:,1],
            c=clusters)

plt.show()

Interpretation Questions

Ask:

  • Do groups separate clearly?
  • Which observations are unusual?
  • Are clusters stable?

Important Lesson

Visualization simplifies reality.

Simplification may hide important information.

14. Cluster Applications in Economics

Economists use clustering for:

  • market segmentation
  • regional analysis
  • poverty profiling
  • firm classification
  • macroeconomic typologies
  • labor market analysis

Example

Countries may cluster into:

  • stable advanced economies
  • vulnerable emerging economies
  • commodity-dependent economies

Important Warning

Labels may shape policy decisions.

Cluster interpretation has political consequences.

15. Limitations of Clustering

Clustering has major limitations.

Important Concerns

Clusters depend on:

  • variable selection
  • scaling
  • algorithm choice
  • number of clusters
  • preprocessing decisions

Critical Lesson

Clusters are:

constructed

NOT:

objectively discovered

Example

Different variables produce different groupings.

Important Question

Are clusters:

  • meaningful?
  • stable?
  • useful?

or merely:

artifacts of modeling choices?

20. Live Coding Session

Activity Title

Clustering Countries by Macroeconomic Characteristics

Step 1 — Import Libraries

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

Step 2 — Load Dataset

data = pd.read_csv("country_macro_data.csv")

Step 3 — Select Variables

X = data[["Inflation",
          "GDP_Growth",
          "Debt",
          "Unemployment"]]

Step 4 — Train K-Means Model

kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3)

kmeans.fit(X)

Step 5 — Extract Cluster Labels

clusters = kmeans.labels_

Step 6 — Visualize Clusters

plt.scatter(data["Inflation"],
            data["GDP_Growth"],
            c=clusters)

plt.show()

Step 7 — Apply PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=2)

principal_components = pca.fit_transform(X)

Step 8 — Visualize PCA Output

plt.scatter(principal_components[:,0],
            principal_components[:,1],
            c=clusters)

plt.show()

Step 9 — Interpretation Questions

Ask students:

  • What economic groups emerge?
  • Are clusters stable?
  • Which countries appear unusual?
  • How sensitive are clusters to variable choice?

24. Common Errors

Problem 1 — Ignoring Scaling

Variables with larger scales may dominate clustering.

Problem 2 — Treating Clusters as Objective Truth

Clusters depend heavily on modeling choices.

Problem 3 — Arbitrary Interpretation

Cluster labels require careful economic reasoning.

Problem 4 — Choosing Too Many Clusters

Too many clusters reduce interpretability.

Problem 5 — Blind Trust in Visualization

Visual separation may exaggerate actual structure.

25. AI Reflection Question

AI systems can automatically generate clusters.

However:

  • AI may create arbitrary segmentation
  • AI may reinforce stereotypes
  • AI may generate unstable groupings

Reflection question:

Why should economists critically evaluate clustering results rather than treating algorithmic groups as objective truths?

  • K-Means clustering

  • limitations of clustering
  • clustering applications in economics
